coverage: Seven stories · AI, security, science and society

cards.headline: Schools get a new AI privacy standard
cards.summary: The AFT, UFT and Microsoft announced a national AI safety and privacy standard for schools. The agreement says participating tools should not use student data to train AI, should not track students, and should keep humans responsible for important decisions.
cards.whyItMatters: Rules about data collection and automated decisions shape how AI can be used in classrooms.

csp.connection: Computing systems affect privacy, access, and decisions about people.

cards.headline: GitHub can block leaked secrets before merge
cards.summary: GitHub added a public-preview repository rule that can stop a pull request from merging when secret scanning finds a newly exposed credential. The rule waits for a scan of the head commit and requires introduced alerts to be resolved first.
cards.whyItMatters: An API key or password accidentally committed to code can become a real security problem, so automated checks can catch mistakes before release.

csp.connection: Authentication secrets control access between users, programs, and network services.

cards.headline: OpenAI adds safety researcher to its board
cards.summary: OpenAI appointed AI safety researcher Paul Christiano to its Foundation Board and Safety and Security Committee. He will also be a non-voting observer on the company board and brings experience evaluating advanced AI systems at NIST.
cards.whyItMatters: AI safety is partly a technical problem and partly a governance problem: people and institutions decide which risks get measured and acted on.

csp.connection: The effects of computing depend on technical choices and on the organizations that govern them.

cards.headline: Apple turns more sensor data into health insights
cards.summary: Apple announced new health features for Apple Watch and a redesigned Health app that uses Apple Intelligence. The company says newer watches will collect higher-frequency heart-rate variability data and offer a readiness score; some features vary by device, age, region, or language.
cards.whyItMatters: Wearables turn streams of sensor measurements into conclusions, which makes data quality, algorithms, privacy, and limits important.

csp.connection: Computers collect, process, and interpret data to produce information people use for decisions.

cards.headline: U.S. and China clash over AI distillation
cards.summary: U.S. agencies accused several China-based AI companies of industrial-scale distillation, using outputs from advanced U.S. models to help train other models while allegedly bypassing access rules. China rejected the accusations and said distillation is a common AI technique.
cards.whyItMatters: A model’s outputs can become training data for another model, raising technical questions about learning and policy questions about access, ownership, and fair use.

csp.connection: Computing innovations can create conflicts over ownership, access, competition, and rules.

cards.headline: AI helps run repetitive quantum-computing experiments
cards.summary: OpenAI described an MIT graduate student connecting GPT-5.6 Sol through Codex to laboratory software for routine quantum-chip measurements. The case study says the system helped run and refine repetitive measurements while the researcher focused on experiment design and data analysis.
cards.whyItMatters: AI agents become more powerful when they can use software tools, but humans still need to set goals, check results, and understand the experiment.

csp.connection: Programs can combine algorithms with tools and feedback to carry out multi-step tasks.

cards.headline: OpenAI funds research on teens and AI
cards.summary: OpenAI announced $5 million for independent research on how generative AI affects people ages 13 to 17. The program asks researchers to study areas such as learning, creativity, advice-seeking, relationships, and how effects differ across teens and situations.
cards.whyItMatters: Students your age are already part of the AI story, and better evidence can help schools, families, and developers make decisions instead of relying only on guesses.

csp.connection: Studying computing’s effects requires evidence about how technology changes people and communities.
